poem:

’Twas cupricnight, the fettlebrims  
Did snush and drindle in the fray;  
All drossy were the ladleims—  
And waxlets piped away.

Beware the Sprue Tree, drippish child!  
The spangling sprong, the molten yawn!  
Beware the Ventyvold, so wild!  
Beware the Spatterpawn!

He took his flitting flasket up;  
Long time he eyed the glazedous spill,  
Then stood beside the burning cup,  
To test his tinker’s skill.

And as in wishful muse he cast,  
The Sprue Tree, slick with glowing skin,  
Came slurking up the vents at last—  
Its branches thin as sin!

One, two! One, two! And through and through  
The shiver-strickle blade he pressed!  
He snuffed the wax, then squirled anew  
With bubble in his vest.

"And hast thou slain the Sprue Tree? Spright!  
Come pour, thou gallant found’rer, pour!"  
He chortled bold in pouring light  
And finned the form once more.

’Twas cupricnight, the fettlebrims  
Did snush and drindle in the fray;  
All drossy were the ladleims—  
And waxlets piped away.

poem:
**Kintsugibandic Gleam**

’Twas brittlebrash, the teapot shards  
Did gyre and glint upon the floor;  
All splinterfray the porcelain hearts,  
And glazelets cracked galore.

Beware the seam of Kintsugold!  
The mender’s hands, the lacquered gleam!  
Beware the crokeld chinnery old,  
The timeworn’s silent seam.

He took his brush of resin gold—  
Long time the fragile foe he faced—  
So rested he by saucer-stone  
And puzzled how they braced.

And as in sequindoubt he knelt,  
The tinsel-bright, with gilded grin,  
Came snick-snick-smoothing through the delft  
And joined the breaks within!

Snap! crack! and soothe, the goldthread danced,  
And soldered clash with subtle art;  
He pieced the jagged sorrowess  
And held its gleaming heart.

’Twas brittlebrash, the teapot whole,  
Did shimmer-mend at dusk of old;  
O fractured joy, the beauty bold  
Of every seam of gold.

Did snerve and shimmer so—

Of crimson’s bloffering glow.

The skaddle-shanks who slide,

The gurpling slope and tide!

And watched the peaks aglow.

Down graddled slopes of gree,  
With blimmerswirl and quaggle-brush  
He stumbled on the scree!  

Skee-flack! Skee-flack! The jagged cracks!  
His walpen-skiff did spring!  
He splundered through the whirlig snaks  
And heard the mountains sing.  

“Come gladden forth your bramble-heart!”  
His shadow fluffed anew;  
’Twas thriftle-morn, the world apart  
In alpenglow and dew.  

So bluffer on, ye trindle-knolls!  
Let corvill skies now be—  
While snerve and spangle, blush and roll  
The alpenglow on scree.

’Twas bramble-cold, and the plane iron  
Did grindle-gleam through furry pine:  
All stringle were the shoflecorn,  
And whingly clanked the line.

“Beware the Ironcamber, son!  
The teeth that gnash, the sole that sneds!  
Beware the chip-curl’s gnarble run,  
The shavings’ silken threads!”

He gribbed his bevel-bladed plane—  
Long time the snickle foe he sought—  
So rested he by trollop tree,  
And cambered deep in thought.

And as in grumbly muse he stood,  
The Ironcamber, smooth and stout,  
With fuzzle-rush through trembling wood  
Came planing, plane about!

Snap-wrack! Snap-wrack! And ravel-swipe!  
His knuckle-knuckle wrath went crack!  
He left it snapped, and with a yipe  
He curled his wood-strewn stack.

“And hast thou slain the Ironcamber?  
Come to my arms, my brambly boy!  
O wondrous day! Frooloo! Frambar!”  
He chortled in his joy.

’Twas bramble-cold, and the plane iron  
Did grindle-gleam through furry pine:  
All stringle were the shoflecorn,  
And whingly clanked the line.
